full_judgment:
4. Brief facts for disposal of the Rule issued in Writ Petition No.9221 of 2008 are that the petitioner is the elected Chairman of No.6 Kulsha Union Parishad under Upazila Kotalipara, District: Gopalgonj. He is a popular political personality being local leader of the Bangladesh Awami League and involved in many social welfare activities. He worked in favour of the Bangladesh Awami League nominated candidate in the last Parliament Election held on October 1, 2001 and incurred displeasure of local leaders of the then ruling party, who were trying to oust the petitioner from the post of Chairman by any means since the day one. Ultimately they were successful to lodge a false criminal case by prevailing upon the Executive Engineer of the Local Government Engineering Department, Gopalgonj being Kotalipara PS Case No. 1 dated 1-10-2004 under section 379 of the Penal Code. 

 5. That in connection with that criminal case the petitioner was removed from his office of Chairman by the respondent No.1 by a letter under memo dated 11-4-2005 issued purportedly under the signature of the respondent No.2. Thereafter the petitioner preferred this writ petition and obtained the present Rule. 

 7. The petitioner is a very popular and highly respected political personality of his locality. He comes of a very respectable family of the locality. The petitioner was the staunch supporter and worker of the elected Member of Parliament late Shah ASM Kibria, former Finance Minister of Bangladesh and this is why the then local leaders of BNP-led 4-party alliance government have falsely implicated him in different criminal cases and the petitioner is on bail in all the criminal cases and he had not been found guilty in any of those criminal cases and some of the cases are still under trial in different courts at Habiganj. 

 9. Mr Abdul Matin Khasru, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the petitioners in both the petitions after taking us through the entire writ petitions, impugned orders and supplementary affidavits, mainly submitted that the respondents have not made any independent inquiry, nor even felt the necessity to issue show cause notice to the petitioners nor had they heard the petitioners in person for forming an opinion whether the allegation of the aforesaid criminal cases were at all justified. Therefore, there is no reasonable basis or materials before the Government to form opinion for suspension and, as such, the impugned orders are arbitrary, malafide and have been passed without lawful authority. 

 10. The learned Advocate next submitted that the sole basis of passing the impugned orders of suspension are on the basis of criminal cases pending against the petitioners at the behest of some vested interested quarters and there is every chance of the petitioners to be found innocent, if the investigation is made properly. 

 11. Lastly, he cited a decision reported in 1994 Lokman Patwari vs Government of Bangladesh 46 DLR (AD) 163 and submitted that mere existence of any of the three circumstances mentioned in section 65(1) of the Ordinance, 1983, will not be enough for taking action against the chairman, government must also form opinion by applying its independent mind in terms of the language mentioned in section 65(1). While forming such opinion Government must establish the essence of section 65(1) considering the materials before the Government those have causal connection with opinion to be formed by the Government. In the instant case the government did not form any opinion in respect of suspension of the petitioners from the office of the Chairman of said Union Parishads. 

 12. Moreover, the learned Counsel referring Annexures-B, C and D series of the supplementary affidavits in Writ Petition No.4789 of 2008 submitted that all the cases mentioned in the impugned orders of suspension are pending before the different Courts. He also submitted that in all those cases, filed against the petitioner, he is on bail and the cases have no nexus with the affairs of the Union Parishad. 

 13. Mr Md Ismail Miah, the learned Counsel on the other hand, by filing affidavit-in-opposition in Writ Petition No.4789 of 2008 on behalf of the respondent No.5 opposes the Rule and submitted that the petitioner is habituated in involving with so many crimes in the locality and many criminal cases are pending against him including offence of capital punishment and is always involved in the activities prejudicial to the interest of the Union Parishad. He further submitted that the petitioner was rightly suspended on 19-6-2008 by the respondent No .2 as per section 65(1) of the Union Parishad Ordinance. He also submitted that the petitioner suppressed the fact that prior to the issuance of Rule, the office of Chairman was handed over. 

 15. The moot question facing this Court in both the writ petitions is, whether the suspension of the petitioners under section 65(1) of Ordinance is justified under the facts and circumstances of each case. 

 "65(1) Where any proceedings have been initiated for the removal of the Chair-man under section 12 or where any criminal proceedings under any law have been started against such Chairman or where on an enquiry by the Government, he is found to be guilty of any misconduct within the meaning of section 12(1) and in the opinion of the Government, the exercise of power by him as Chairman is either likely to be prejudicial to the interest of the Union Parishad or undesirable from the point of view of public interest, the Government may, by order in writing, place such Chairman under suspension; and during the period of suspension, an Acting Chairman elected in accordance with the provisions of section 16 shall discharge the functions of the Chairman until the termination of the proceedings or, in the event of the Chairman being removed as a result of such proceedings, or until the suspension is withdrawn or until a new Chairman is elected for the Union Parishad....(2) when an order of suspension has been made under sub-section (1), the Chairman shall, not later than three days from the date of communication of the order, make over charge of his office to the Acting Chairman to discharge the functions of the Chairman" 

 17. In these cases though the Chairman was alleged to have committed offences which were serious in nature, but his performance of functions of the Union Parishad would not be prejudiced as in these cases there was no nexus between the Chairman's alleged criminal act and his in performing functions as Chairman of the Union Parishad. Therefore the said cases do not come within the mischief of section 65(1) of the Local Government (Union Parishad) Ordinance, 1983. 

 18. In the case of 46 DLR (AD) 163 Bangladesh vs Lokman Patzvari it was held that, 

 19. It is held in the above decision that mere existence of any of the three circumstance appearing in the section 65(1) of the Local Government (Union Parishad) Ordinance, 1983 is not sufficient to suspend the Chairman. In that case the Chairman implicated on a charge of murder and yet the order of suspending the Chairman was held to be without lawful authority. 

 20. In the case of Md Abdul Hye Bhuiyan vs Secretary, Ministry of Local Government and Rural Development and Co-operative 1981 BLD (AD) /96 the petitioner was accused of offences under sections 147/148/449/326/309/379 of the Penal Code. In that case it was held that the impugned order did not reveal either the application of mind to the criminal proceeding and its effect on the exercise of power by the Chairman or forming of any opinion on it and therefore could not be sustained in law. 

 21. It is not found that in the present cases before us that show cause notice was issued upon the petitioners nor had they been heard in person for forming an opinion. If the respondents asked the petitioners to show cause or would have heard in person or would have held an independent inquiry it would have been found that the whole case is false, fabricated and concocted. To appreciate the contention of the learned Counsel we find no enquiry was held at any point of time before making suspension, neither the petitioners were given a chance to show cause asking reason against the allegation so made in the impugned order of suspension. So, we find substance in the submissions of the learned Counsel for the petitioners that the impugned orders have been passed without making proper enquiry and without giving opportunity to show cause or being heard in person. Therefore there is no reasonable basis or materials before the government to form opinion for suspension of the petitioners. In the decision of Shaik Abdul Quader vs Chairman, Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation reported in 30 DLR (SC) 96 it was held that before an order of suspension against a public servant is passed he should be given an opportunity as a matter of right to explain allegations against him.
